source: Constantinescu, O'Reilly, Behrens (2016) Organizing conceptual knowledge in humans with a gridlike code
finding: Humans moved through an abstract 2-D 'bird space' (neck and leg length) and showed a six-fold (hexagonal) fMRI signal in medial prefrontal and entorhinal cortex, the signature used as a proxy for grid cells.
numbers: N=28 fMRI subjects; 72.8 +/- 1.0% accuracy predicting outcomes; 0 of 28 reported thinking of a spatial map. Entorhinal peak Z=4.41, vmPFC Z=4.09. Session-to-session grid-angle consistency: vmPFC t26=2.61, ERH t27=2.36 (both p<0.05); across sessions more than a week apart vmPFC t20=3.65 (p<0.01).
limits: Signal is indirect (fMRI, not single cells). Entorhinal map used a more lenient threshold (Z=2.3). Small sample; the space was smooth, continuous and 2-D. Cross-day tests used 20 to 22 subjects.
agent_relevance: Evidence that relational structure can be coded with map-like geometry when it is continuous and 2-D. It does not show this for discrete, high-dimensional task graphs, so S2 should not assume a geometric map for every task.

source: Constantinescu, O'Reilly, Behrens (2016) Organizing conceptual knowledge in humans with a gridlike code (control periodicities and behaviour link)
finding: The effect was specific to six-fold symmetry, not four-, five-, seven- or eight-fold. People with stronger hexagonal modulation in vmPFC did better on the task.
numbers: Control periodicities all p>0.15 (within day) and p>0.18 (across days). Hexagonal modulation vs accuracy r=0.432, p=0.039; consistency vs accuracy r=0.431, p=0.039 (N about 28).
limits: Brain-behaviour correlations at p=0.039 with N=28 are fragile. Learning speed during training did not predict the signal.
agent_relevance: Map quality links to task performance, so a quality check on the map (does it predict held-out moves?) is a sensible gate before planning from it.

source: Garvert, Dolan, Behrens (2017) A map of abstract relational knowledge in the human hippocampal-entorhinal cortex (eLife, with post-review revision)
finding: Participants saw object sequences from a random walk on a 10-node graph with no instruction. Entorhinal/hippocampal adaptation tracked graph distance, and a separate behavioural group showed matching reaction-time distance effects. The revised paper reports no evidence for mapping discrete links into Euclidean space; the data fit a predictive (successor-like) code.
numbers: fMRI N=23 (mean age 23.5); behavioural group N=26 (10 or 12 blocks, 127 objects per block, each transition probed 30 times). In a null set of 68,295 link-permuted graphs, only 13.17% had no line crossings (a test for a flat 2-D map).
quote: We found no evidence for a mapping of discrete relationships into Euclidian space.
limits: Small sample; graph had only a few nodes. Reinterpretation came after review.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the 'map' for discrete relational structure looks predictive and distorted by visit frequency, not a faithful picture of the graph. For S2, store how often or how likely transitions are, not only edges.

source: Garvert et al. (2017) revision: communicability as rival to shortest-path distance
finding: Added analysis: a communicability measure (matrix exponential of the graph) fitted the neural adaptation signal better than shortest-path length. It shortens links that sit on many paths and lengthens rarely used ones.
numbers: Communicability has no free parameter and falls with graph distance. Null model with 68,295 graphs.
limits: Post-hoc reinterpretation on N=23; both readings fit one small dataset.
agent_relevance: A rival theory (predictive code vs geometric map) changes what S2 should store: transition frequency matters as well as links.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning (Nat Hum Behav), Experiment 1
finding: In a passive learning task (N=58) people updated their start-state preference after a reward change more than after a transition change, as a successor representation predicts. They still updated after transition changes, so behaviour is not purely SR.
numbers: Revaluation score: reward .5199 (SEM .0203), transition .4503 (SEM .0229), control .0310. Reward vs transition t(57)=2.89, Bonferroni p=0.016; each vs control t(57)=10.14 and 9.05, p<.001; ANOVA F(2,1154)=38.77.
limits: The reward-transition gap is small (about 0.07). Behaviour is semi-flexible, so it does not isolate one map type. Passive task, simple trees.
agent_relevance: Humans partly cache predictions about future states. A scaffold that replans from a stored map should expect stale caches after the world changes and force a re-derive step on a transition change.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017), Experiment 2 (sequential decision, instrumental)
finding: Replicated and extended Exp 1 with action choices and a new policy-revaluation condition. People switched their first-stage choice most after reward change, less after transition or policy change.
numbers: N=88. Proportion switching: reward .6591, transition .4659, policy .5000, control .0795. Reward vs transition Wald Z=-2.85, p=.0034; reward vs policy Z=-2.61, p=.0043; policy vs transition p=.5771.
limits: One probe trial per condition gives noisy binary data. A hybrid model was needed to explain the policy result.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the agent checks what changed (reward vs structure) before deciding how much of its map to rebuild.

source: Butler, Hardcastle, Giocomo (2019) Remembered reward locations restructure entorhinal spatial maps (Science)
finding: When rats had to go to a remembered reward zone, medial entorhinal grid, head-direction, border and other spatial maps re-organised relative to free foraging in a different box: grids rotated, rescaled and became less elliptical, and decoding of position near the reward improved.
numbers: 7 rats, 778 cells recorded in both boxes; 102 grid cells. Median absolute grid rotation 12.53 deg (p=1.1e-12); 49 of 102 grid cells changed significantly on at least one measure; 70 of 132 HD cells changed tuning; 196 of 271 non-grid spatial cells remapped (task-trained mean r 0.32 vs control 0.41; 49 of 100 control cells remapped). Training took a mean of 15 sessions (range 8 to 24).
limits: Control group was only 3 rats, and grid spacing change did not differ between groups. This shows task demands reshape the map; it does not show a smooth skew of fields toward the goal. Rats.
agent_relevance: The map is goal-shaped, not neutral: what you plan for changes how the state space is carved. S2 should build the representation conditioned on the goal, not one generic map.

source: Whittington et al. (2020) The Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine: Unifying Space and Relational Memory through Generalization in the Hippocampal Formation (Cell)
finding: A model that learns structure separately from sensory content reproduces grid, band, border and object-vector cells and place/landmark cells, and predicts that hippocampal remapping keeps structure across environments. It also covers non-spatial tasks such as laps with a reward every 4th lap.
numbers: Authors report confirming the structure-preserving remapping prediction in simultaneously recorded place and grid cells (counts not read). The model learns 'every 4 laps' entorhinal cells that were predicted but not yet recorded.
limits: A model fitted to reproduce known cell types, not a decisive test against rivals such as the successor-representation account.
agent_relevance: Recipe: separate reusable structure (the map) from specific content (names, objects) and bind them. Matches S2 as a reusable map of states and moves.

source: Whittington, McCaffary, Bedford, Behrens (2022) Relating transformers to models and neural representations of the hippocampal formation (ICLR)
finding: A transformer with recurrent position encodings (TEM-t) learns place and grid-like representations, is closely related to the neuroscience TEM, and learns more efficiently.
numbers: TEM-t needs many fewer samples and less training time than TEM (Figure 4a,b); it can store and retrieve many more memories. Exact ratios not read.
limits: Position encoding was chosen to make this work. Match to neurons is by representation, not a causal test. Not tested on language tasks.
agent_relevance: A link between transformer attention and hippocampal map-building, so LLMs can plausibly hold a map in context if the structure is given.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in Large Language Models with CogEval
finding: Eight LLMs were tested on planning over graphs described in words (rooms, social ties, object relations) with repeated trials. They looked competent only on simple graphs and failed with hallucinated edges, longer than shortest paths, and loops.
numbers: Logistic regression: temperature not significant (chi2(11)=1.28, p=.53); LLM chi2(11)=2357.87, graph chi2(11)=3431.53, condition chi2(11)=2080.04, domain chi2(11)=304.06, all p<.001. GPT-4-32k odds multiple 3.50 vs Alpaca-7B baseline. Shortest path to a state 1 cluster away on community graphs: GPT-4 succeeded 0 of 30 at temperature 0, at most 10% at other temperatures.
quote: LLMs display the following failure modes; (1) hallucinate edges that do not exist, or (2) fall into longer trajectories
limits: 2023 models (GPT-4, Claude-1, Bard, LLaMA). Graph given in text. Newer reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Core negative result for S2: giving the model the edges in text does not give it a usable map. It lists edges well but fails to use them. Argues for an explicit, checked map and a validity test on every proposed move.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval, Experiment 2: BFS/DFS instructions
finding: Adding a short description of breadth-first or depth-first search to the GPT-4 prompt helped only in some community-graph tasks, and not consistently across temperature.
numbers: 30 repeats per prompt and temperature. BFS best for within-cluster shortest path at temperature 0; for shortest path 1 cluster away only BFS at temperature 0.5 helped; cluster counting improved at temperatures 0 and 0.5 but less at 1.
limits: Authors call effects 'not consistent nor monotonic'. Exact rates only in figures.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to search is weak. Run the procedure as code or a checked step list rather than asking in prose (supports a graph-search operator).

source: Kim et al. (2024) How language models extrapolate outside the training data: a case study in Textualized Gridworld
finding: A 'cognitive map' chain of thought (build a map of the grid, then plan from it), trained into Llama-3-8B, lifts path planning in larger unseen grids far above plain next-token and ordinary CoT training.
numbers: Optimal-plan rate: no CoT 19.0%, best explicit CoT 26.5%, cognitive map 76.5% (BWD UNMARK). Reachable-plan rate: 32.1%, 33.9%, 88.5% (BWD MARK). Maps keep over 40% success at complexity 25 vs training max 15.
limits: Needed fine-tuning. A depth-first exploration baseline reached 94.5% reachability vs 88.5% for the map. Toy gridworld only.
agent_relevance: A map-first step helps when the model has a trained habit for it, and plain search can match it. Supports S2 as a cheap map plus a search operator.

source: Kim et al. (2024), prompting-only test of the cognitive-map format
finding: Few-shot prompting for the cognitive-map format did not work in any tested model (Llama-3 8B and 70B, GPT-4o, GPT-o1). Only GPT-o1 with plain no-CoT prompting did meaningfully.
numbers: GPT-o1 no-CoT: 0%, 18%, 34%, 38% at 0, 1, 2, 4 shots. Cognitive-map prompting: 0 to 1% for most models, at most 10% for one model at 4 shots. Ordinary CoT prompting: at most 10%, one model at 2 shots.
quote: None of the tested foundation models could produce meaningful results for the cognitive map approach through few-shot prompting
limits: The PDF table text was garbled, so row-to-model mapping follows the paper's own text. Small prompt-only sample.
agent_relevance: Warns that asking a model in a prompt to 'draw a map first' is not the same as a trained map habit. A scaffold must check the map, not trust it.

source: Dedieu et al. (2024) Learning Cognitive Maps from Transformer Representations for Efficient Planning in Partially Observed Environments
finding: Plain transformers and LSTMs predict the next observation almost perfectly in aliased rooms but fail at path planning by forward rollout. A transformer with discrete bottlenecks yields a map that, with an external solver, finds shortest paths.
numbers: Averages over 10 aliased 15x20 rooms with 4 observations: LSTM test accuracy 99.00% but beats a fallback path only 29.53% of the time, with paths 16.82 times longer than optimal. Best bottleneck variants: about 99% accuracy, 96.59 to 99.55% improvement over fallback, shortest-path ratio 1.00. A too-simple variant improved only 6.61% of the time and merged look-alike states into false shortcuts.
limits: Synthetic rooms. Needs training and an external graph solver.
agent_relevance: Next-step accuracy does not imply planning ability. Keep prediction (the model) apart from search (the solver), and merge look-alike states with care (aliasing creates false shortcuts).

source: Park et al. (2025) ICLR: In-Context Learning of Representations
finding: When Llama-3.1-8B reads random walks over a graph whose nodes are everyday words, its internal representations switch from the words' pretrained meaning to the graph layout after enough context. Words with correlated meanings (days of the week) resist this.
numbers: Square-grid and ring graphs; analysis windows of 50 preceding tokens; context lengths shown from 200 to 1400 tokens; structure appears abruptly with more context. Also tested on Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B.
limits: Toy graphs, open models up to 8B. Representation analysis, not planning performance. Semantic prior can dominate.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a map can form inside the context given enough walk examples, but old meanings can overpower it. Give many transitions and prefer arbitrary node labels.

source: Baumgartner, Spens, Burgess, Manescu (2025) Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
finding: GPT-2 models trained only to predict random-walk steps in a grid develop a map-like coordinate system; models trained to output shortest paths do not and stay dependent on direction tokens. Training data type decides which.
numbers: Foraging model: 100% at 2 to 3 steps, 71% near 11 steps, over 96% beyond 30 steps. Shortest-path model on Hamiltonian paths: 100% in-distribution, 0% at other context lengths. Hybrid model kept over 97% at long context. Goal-directed models: 17.38% average on one test, 78% on edge-to-edge paths. Direction patching worked in 97.4% of trials.
limits: Small GPT-2 models trained from scratch on grids, not pretrained LLMs.
agent_relevance: Training on exploration gives maps; training on goal paths gives brittle shortcuts. For a no-training scaffold, argues for an explicit exploration and mapping stage before goal search.

source: Baumgartner et al. (2025), phase transition result
finding: In the foraging model, reliance on earlier direction tokens vanishes by the middle layers, meaning it stores a position, not the path history. Goal-directed models never do this.
numbers: Ablating direction tokens at layer 8 or later left accuracy at 100%; early ablation hurt. The model switches between a low-level heuristic for short contexts and map inference for long ones.
limits: Small custom 12-layer networks; layer numbers do not transfer.
agent_relevance: Position-state versus path-history is the real test of a map: the scaffold can check whether the state summary alone suffices to continue the plan.

source: Qin, Cohen, Reddy (2026) Cognitive Maps in Large Language Models
finding: Open-weight models above about 10 billion parameters infer unstated relations (family trees and other structures), generalise to made-up names, and hold abstract structure and entity identity as separate, added codes. Facts are kept as pairwise links composed at query time, not placed in a global coordinate frame.
numbers: Models: Gemma-3 (4B, 12B, 27B), Llama-3.1 (8B, 70B), Qwen3 (0.6B to 32B, thinking off); 50 trials per condition in mosaic (activation-swap) tests; binding by sparse sites, about 1% of keys and values; implanted 'false memories' shifted answers predictably.
limits: Preprint dated 19 Oct 2026. Relational reasoning in text, not planning. 'Analogous to a cognitive map' is the authors' reading; the code is pairwise, unlike a metric map.
agent_relevance: Strong models can compose a stated relation chain, so they can read a map, but they do not hold a global layout. An external explicit map for long routes (S2) is still justified; small models need it more.

source: Gurnee and Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time (ICLR)
finding: Linear probes recover place coordinates and dates from middle layers of Llama-2 models, across world, US and NYC places and historical, entertainment and headline dates.
numbers: Out-of-sample R2 at 60% depth, linear probe, Llama-2-7b: world 0.881, US 0.799, NYC 0.219, historical 0.785, entertainment 0.788, headlines 0.564. Last linear row (largest model, label garbled): 0.911, 0.864, 0.359, 0.835, 0.885, 0.746.
limits: Probes show information is present, not that the model uses it for planning. Fine-grained NYC places are weak (R2 0.22 to 0.36).
agent_relevance: LLMs encode coarse geography, so a map of a familiar domain is partly in the weights. For a novel task graph the map must be built in context.

source: Li et al. (2023) Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task (Othello-GPT)
finding: A GPT trained only on legal Othello moves builds an internal board-state representation that nonlinear probes can read and interventions can change, which changes its predicted moves.
numbers: Legal-move error rate: 0.01% (synthetic data), 5.17% (championship data), untrained 93.29%. Linear probes never fell below about 20% error; nonlinear probes were much better; randomised-network baseline near chance.
limits: Rule-defined board with a small state space. Not about natural-language planning.
agent_relevance: A next-token model can learn a state map when states are well defined and data is rich. Supports giving the model a state-and-moves format to fill (S2).

source: Liu et al. (2026) MAP: A Map-then-Act Paradigm for Long-Horizon Interactive Agent Reasoning
finding: Making the agent explore and write a structured map of the environment before acting beats step-by-step ReAct, and beats mixing mapping into acting (CoMAP), on ALFWorld, TextCraft and ScienceWorld.
numbers: Success rates (table parsed from PDF, approximate), ReAct -> MAP: Qwen3-4B-Instruct ALFWorld 31.8 -> 61.1, TextCraft 31.8 -> 71.9, SciWorld 13.9 -> 24.3. Qwen3-4B-Thinking 58.5 -> 71.5, 35.6 -> 59.6, 1.5 -> 11.4. Strong models near 99 gain little. On ARC-AGI-3, Claude 4.6 Opus went from near zero under ReAct to improvements in 22 of 25 games (levels in Table 2, not read).
limits: Preprint, not replicated. Gains largest for small models. ARC-AGI-3 gains are from a near-zero base.
agent_relevance: Close match to S2 ahead of acting: build the map first, then act. Timing matters (ReAct < CoMAP < MAP), not just map presence.

source: Yan (2025) External Hippocampus: Topological Cognitive Maps for Guiding LLM Reasoning
finding: Builds a graph of reasoning states from embeddings and injects prompts or temperature perturbations when the trace gets stuck. Reported gains on small models.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-3B: 64.40% single inference to 81.20% with map-guided iterative refinement (about 2.52 rounds), while CoT self-consistency (k=5) scored 59.80%. Phi-3-mini: 68.0% to 71.4%. 500 problems.
limits: Single author, small models, no replication. 'Cognitive map' here is a graph of embedding states, not a map of the task; the biology link is a metaphor.
agent_relevance: The term 'cognitive map' is used loosely in LLM work. Check that a method really uses task structure before counting it as evidence for S2.

source: Gershman (2018) The Successor Representation: Its Computational Logic and Neural Substrates (J Neurosci)
finding: Review of the successor representation, which stores each state by the states likely to follow it. Argues it accounts for place and grid firing and trades flexibility against efficiency. Abstract only.
numbers: No numbers taken from the abstract.
limits: Abstract only was read; the review's caveats were not.
agent_relevance: Frames the map as a cached forecast of where moves lead: cheap, but stale when transitions change.

source: Social hierarchy grid-like code study (2020 bioRxiv, 'Inferences on a Multidimensional Social Hierarchy Use a Grid-like Code')
finding: Reports that discrete relations between people in an unseen 2-D social hierarchy were rebuilt into a 2-D map in hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, with a grid-like code for inferred trajectories. Abstract only.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Abstract only. Author list not verified. Same fMRI method as the 2016 study, so not fully independent.
agent_relevance: Another positive case for a 2-D map built from discrete facts by inference.

source: vmPFC null result (2019 bioRxiv, 'Subjective value, not a gridlike code, describes neural activity in vmPFC during value-based decision-making')
finding: Reports no significant hexagonal grid-like signal in vmPFC in a large intertemporal-choice fMRI dataset; subjective value fitted better. Authors suggest vmPFC switches coding scheme to suit the task. Abstract only.
numbers: Abstract states 'no significant evidence at all' for a hexagonal code; sample size not recorded.
limits: Abstract only. Different task (choice among options, not movement through a space), so it limits generality rather than refuting 2016. Authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Boundary: the grid-like code appears when the task is traversing a space. Do not assume a map is used for every decision.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Distance and grid-like codes support the navigation of abstract social space in the human brain (eLife)
finding: People learned a 2-D social space (competence by warmth) and navigated to learned locations. Distance was coded in precuneus, fusiform and occipital areas. Grid-like evidence was only partial: no entorhinal region survived the main whole-region test.
numbers: N=38 included after excluding accuracy under 60% in the scanner (15 males, mean age 21.47). In entorhinal subregions, 31 participants showed clustered voxel orientations (V-test, all p<0.040), but the pmEC ROI was 'less consistent'.
quote: partial evidence of grid-like representation patterns
limits: Reviewers noted that real social, semantic and navigation spaces are higher-dimensional, so a clean six-fold code is not expected. Authors call the evidence 'partial'.
agent_relevance: Grid-like codes for abstract spaces are weaker and less consistent than the 2016 headline suggests. Do not build the scaffold on a strict geometric grid assumption.

source: Wu et al. (2024) eLife, behaviour and individual differences
finding: Strength of the grid-like response scaled with navigation performance and with a social avoidance trait score. Low performers were excluded.
numbers: 38 kept of the scanned sample; pilot ratings from an independent online sample of 39 participants matched avatar traits.
limits: Exclusion on performance may favour people who built a map. Correlations in small samples.
agent_relevance: Only some people build a clean map. A scaffold that forces an explicit map may help weaker builders, like a prosthetic.
